questions.question: Which event was contested at the Olympics from 1900 to 1920 but never returned as a regular discipline?

answers.text: Tug of war
Stone lifting
Log throwing

questions.fun_fact: Britain won all three medals at the 1908 Games because teams entered as separate London police units — City Police took gold, Liverpool Police silver, and Metropolitan Police K Division bronze.

questions.question: At which Olympics were live animals shot for medals as an officially contested event?

answers.text: Paris 1900
Athens 1896
St. Louis 1904

questions.fun_fact: Live pigeon shooting featured nearly 300 birds shot from cages. Belgian Leon de Lunden won with 21 kills. It was the only Olympics where animals were intentionally killed for sport.

questions.question: What unusual feat did Eric Moussambani from Equatorial Guinea achieve at the Sydney 2000 Olympics?

answers.text: He won his 100m freestyle heat after both rivals were disqualified — with one of the slowest Olympic times ever
He set a world record despite never training in a 50m pool
He swam the entire race underwater on a single breath

questions.fun_fact: Moussambani had only learned to swim eight months earlier in a 20m hotel pool. He finished in 1:52.72 — slower than most Olympic 200m times — but the crowd of 17,000 gave him a standing ovation.

questions.question: Art competitions — for painting, sculpture, literature, music and architecture — once awarded Olympic medals. When were they last held?

answers.text: London 1948
Berlin 1936
Stockholm 1912

questions.fun_fact: Pierre de Coubertin himself won gold for literature in 1912 under a pseudonym for his poem 'Ode to Sport'. The medals were dropped because most competing artists were professionals, violating amateur rules.

questions.question: Solo synchronised swimming was an Olympic event in 1984, 1988 and 1992. What's odd about its name?

answers.text: A single swimmer was 'synchronising' only with the music
Swimmers competed against their own mirrored reflection
Two athletes performed but only one was scored

questions.fun_fact: Critics mocked the event as the most contradictory in Olympic history. It was dropped after Barcelona 1992 because the IOC added a team event for Atlanta 1996 and chose to keep duet + team rather than carry three sub-disciplines.

questions.question: At the 1904 St. Louis Olympics marathon, the gold medallist nearly died. What had he ingested mid-race?

answers.text: Strychnine mixed with brandy and raw egg whites
Raw opium dissolved in milk
Pure ether on sugar cubes

questions.fun_fact: Thomas Hicks's handlers gave him strychnine — a rat poison that acts as a stimulant in tiny doses — twice during the race. He had to be carried across the line and could not collect his medal in person.

questions.question: Why was the marathon distance fixed at exactly 42.195 km (26 miles 385 yards)?

answers.text: To finish in front of the royal box at the 1908 London Olympics
It was the exact distance from Marathon to Athens in 490 BC
Pierre de Coubertin picked it from a hat at random

questions.fun_fact: The original 1896 marathon was only about 40 km. The 1908 London course was extended so the start was at Windsor Castle and the finish lay before Queen Alexandra's box at White City Stadium. The IAAF fixed it permanently in 1921.

questions.question: Which Olympic event was scored purely on how far a motionless diver drifted underwater after entering the pool?

answers.text: Plunge for distance (no kicking, no swimming, only the dive's momentum counted)
Tandem cycling sprint
Rope climbing for style

questions.fun_fact: At St. Louis 1904, divers leapt in, then floated motionless face-down for 60 seconds. Distance covered by drift was measured. American William Dickey won with 19.05 m. Spectators found it agonisingly dull and it was never repeated.

questions.question: How did the Olympic torch relay originate?

answers.text: It was invented by the Nazi regime for the 1936 Berlin Games
It dates back to the ancient Greek Olympics in Olympia
It started at Athens 1896 as Pierre de Coubertin's idea

questions.fun_fact: Carl Diem designed the relay for Berlin 1936 as propaganda linking the Third Reich to ancient Greece. It was so visually striking that the IOC kept it after the war — the only Nazi-era invention still part of every modern Games.

questions.question: At the 1936 Berlin Olympics, who supposedly handed Jesse Owens his winning long-jump tip in the qualifying round?

answers.text: His German rival Luz Long
American coach Lawson Robertson
Hitler's chauffeur Erich Kempka

questions.fun_fact: Long reportedly advised Owens to take off well before the board to avoid fouling. Owens won gold, Long took silver, and they posed arm-in-arm — a famous photo of friendship across the Nazi regime's racial lines.

questions.question: What do competitors in the annual Cooper's Hill event in Gloucestershire, England, chase down a near-vertical slope?

answers.text: A 3.6 kg wheel of Double Gloucester cheese
A wooden barrel filled with cider
A live greased pig

questions.fun_fact: The cheese reaches over 110 km/h. Winners get to keep the wheel. Broken bones and concussions are so common that ambulances are stationed at the bottom — the race continues anyway.

questions.question: In the sport of Wife Carrying, originating in Finland, what is the traditional prize for the winning couple?

answers.text: The wife's weight in beer
A year's supply of reindeer meat
A wooden sauna shipped to the winner's home

questions.fun_fact: The 'Estonian carry' — wife hanging upside-down on the husband's back with her legs around his neck — was developed for the championships and now dominates because it leaves the carrier's arms free.

questions.question: Chess boxing alternates rounds of chess and boxing. How can a competitor win on the board rather than in the ring?

answers.text: By checkmate or by their opponent running out of chess clock time
Only by forcing a resignation — the clock doesn't apply
By capturing the opponent's queen

questions.fun_fact: Each player has 9 minutes total on the chess clock spread over multiple rounds. After exhausting boxing, players often blunder — heavy breathing and adrenaline ruin board calculation.

questions.question: The longest professional tennis match on record lasted over 11 hours across three days. Where was it played?

answers.text: Wimbledon
US Open
Australian Open

questions.fun_fact: Isner vs Mahut in 2010 ended 70-68 in the fifth set. The scoreboard initially broke because it wasn't programmed for scores that high. Both players received commemorative trophies and Wimbledon later introduced a fifth-set tiebreak rule.

questions.question: What does an 'Iron Man' triathlon involve, in order?

answers.text: 3.86 km swim, 180 km bike, 42.2 km run
5 km swim, 150 km bike, 50 km run
10 km swim, 100 km bike, 40 km run

questions.fun_fact: The format was invented in 1978 during a debate among Hawaiian athletes over who was fittest — swimmers, cyclists or runners. Naval officer John Collins suggested combining all three. Fifteen people started; twelve finished.

questions.question: In the Finnish sport of mobile phone throwing, what category exists alongside 'distance'?

answers.text: Freestyle, judged on aesthetic style of the throw
Accuracy at hitting a phone-shaped target
Maximum number of phones thrown in 60 seconds

questions.fun_fact: The world record for distance is over 110 m. Old Nokias are preferred for their aerodynamics. Organisers say it's a cathartic protest against mobile-phone overuse.

questions.question: Bog snorkelling, an annual race in Wales, has one strict rule about technique. What is it?

answers.text: Competitors may not use conventional swimming strokes — only flipper kicks
Competitors must keep their snorkel above water the entire race
Competitors must swim with their eyes closed

questions.fun_fact: Racers cross 120 yards of murky peat trench twice. The world record is under 1 minute 18 seconds. Wetsuits are optional but strongly advised — the bog water hovers around 10°C.

questions.question: Sepak takraw — popular across Southeast Asia — combines volleyball rules with which forbidden body part rule?

answers.text: Players may not use their hands or arms
Players may not let the ball touch their head
Players must keep one foot on the ground at all times

questions.fun_fact: Played with a woven rattan ball, sepak takraw rewards bicycle kicks across the net from full height. Skilled players spike the ball downward from above the 1.5m net using their feet.

questions.question: Buzkashi, the national sport of Afghanistan, uses what as the 'ball'?

answers.text: A headless goat or calf carcass
A leather sack filled with sand
A wooden cylinder wrapped in sheepskin

questions.fun_fact: Riders on horseback try to drag the 30-50 kg carcass into a scoring circle. Matches can last days. Genghis Khan's cavalry are believed to have played an early form on the Central Asian steppe.

questions.question: Kabaddi, a contact team sport from South Asia, has one peculiar rule about what the attacking 'raider' must do.

answers.text: Continuously chant 'kabaddi' on a single breath while raiding
Carry a small wooden baton at all times
Touch the opposing captain before any other player

questions.fun_fact: If the raider inhales mid-chant, they're out. The sport featured at the 1936 Berlin Olympics as a demonstration event and has been part of the Asian Games since 1990.

questions.question: Which NFL team is the only one publicly owned by its fans rather than a private owner?

answers.text: Green Bay Packers
Pittsburgh Steelers
Cleveland Browns

questions.fun_fact: Over 360,000 shareholders own the Packers. Shares pay no dividend, can't appreciate in value, and can't be resold for profit — yet the team has held six share offerings (1923, 1935, 1950, 1997, 2011, 2021) to fund stadium upgrades.

questions.question: In football (soccer), what was unusual about the rule for goal celebrations until the 1990s in the English league?

answers.text: There was no rule against removing your shirt — bookings for it only began in 2004 worldwide
Goalkeepers were forbidden from celebrating
Players could be fined for shaking the opposing goalkeeper's hand

questions.fun_fact: FIFA introduced the mandatory yellow card for shirt removal in 2004, citing time-wasting and 'unsporting' behaviour. The rule remains controversial — many goalscorers still strip their shirts despite the booking.

questions.question: What did the first FIFA World Cup trophy, the Jules Rimet, suffer in 1966 and 1983?

answers.text: It was stolen twice — recovered once by a dog in 1966, never found after 1983
It was melted down for charity then re-cast in solid bronze
It was struck by lightning during an open-top parade

questions.fun_fact: A dog named Pickles found the trophy under a hedge in South London a week after the 1966 theft. Brazil was given the original permanently after their third win in 1970. It was stolen again from Rio in 1983 and is believed to have been melted down.

questions.question: What is the maximum legal width of an NFL goalpost upright?

answers.text: About 18 feet 6 inches (5.64 m) between uprights
Exactly 12 feet (3.66 m)
Exactly 24 feet (7.32 m), matching football goals

questions.fun_fact: College goalposts are the same width but were 23 feet 4 inches until 1991. NFL kickers complain that even from 60+ yards, the narrow target is psychologically harder than a soccer goal at any distance.

questions.question: Which feature of the modern football was standardised only after the 1970 World Cup?

answers.text: Black-and-white panels (Adidas Telstar) for TV visibility
Synthetic leather replacing real leather
32 panels in any colour scheme

questions.fun_fact: Before the Telstar, balls were plain brown leather, hard to see on black-and-white TV. The 32-panel truncated-icosahedron pattern was designed at Adidas specifically so spectators watching at home could follow the play.

questions.question: How does a 'safety' score points in American football?

answers.text: The defensive team tackles the ball carrier in the offense's own end zone for 2 points
The defence intercepts inside the 5-yard line for 1 point
The defence forces a punt from inside the 10-yard line for 3 points

questions.fun_fact: After conceding a safety, the team must then kick off to the opposition — losing both the points and possession. It's the only score where the defending team also gains the ball.

questions.question: Which footballer holds the record for the fastest red card in a professional match?

answers.text: Lee Todd — sent off after 2 seconds for swearing at the referee
Vinnie Jones — sent off after 5 seconds for a sliding tackle
Pepe — sent off after 8 seconds for headbutting an opponent

questions.fun_fact: Cross Farm Park Celtic player Todd swore loudly after the kickoff whistle startled him in 2000. The referee was within earshot and dismissed him on the spot — before he had even touched the ball.

questions.question: The NFL's 'Heidi Game' in 1968 is remembered for what unusual reason?

answers.text: NBC cut away from the live broadcast to show the film Heidi, missing the entire ending
A snow blizzard during play resembled a scene from Heidi
A goat named Heidi ran onto the field and stopped play

questions.fun_fact: With 65 seconds left and the Jets leading the Raiders, NBC switched to Heidi on schedule. The Raiders scored twice in nine seconds to win 43-32. Viewer outrage led to the 'Heidi Rule' guaranteeing all NFL games are shown to their conclusion.

questions.question: What did the inventor of basketball, James Naismith, use as the first 'baskets' in 1891?

answers.text: Peach baskets nailed to a balcony
Empty barrels set on the floor
Old bicycle wheels with netting attached

questions.fun_fact: Each made basket required someone to climb a ladder and retrieve the ball — they hadn't thought to cut the bottoms out. The bottomless metal hoop arrived in 1906.

questions.question: The Frisbee is named after which real-world object?

answers.text: Pie tins from the Frisbie Pie Company of Connecticut
A Yale dormitory called Frisbee Hall
An Alpine bird called the Frisbean that hovers in updrafts

questions.fun_fact: Yale students tossed empty Frisbie pie tins for fun. Wham-O bought the plastic design in 1957 from a man who had been selling them as 'Pluto Platters', and renamed them Frisbees to match the campus slang.

questions.question: Where were the ancient Olympic Games held continuously for nearly 1,200 years?

answers.text: Olympia, a sanctuary in the western Peloponnese
Mount Olympus in northern Greece
Athens, in the Panathenaic Stadium

questions.fun_fact: The ancient Games ran from 776 BC until they were banned by the Christian emperor Theodosius I in 393 AD. Athletes competed naked, women were banned as spectators, and a sacred truce halted wars across Greece.

questions.question: Volleyball was invented in 1895 as a calmer alternative to which sport for older businessmen?

answers.text: Basketball
Tennis
Handball

questions.fun_fact: YMCA director William G. Morgan invented 'mintonette' so his middle-aged members didn't have to do basketball's physical contact. A spectator suggested 'volleyball' after watching players volley the ball back and forth.

questions.question: The oldest sporting trophy still awarded was first contested in 1851. What is it?

answers.text: The America's Cup (sailing)
The Ashes urn (cricket)
The Stanley Cup (ice hockey)

questions.fun_fact: The schooner America won the trophy off the Isle of Wight in 1851, beating 15 British yachts. The New York Yacht Club held it for 132 years — the longest winning streak in sport — until Australia II broke it in 1983.

questions.question: Modern boxing gloves were popularised because of which rule reform?

answers.text: The Marquess of Queensberry rules of 1867
The Tunney–Dempsey reforms of 1927
The Olympic amateur code of 1904

questions.fun_fact: Bare-knuckle prizefights of the 1800s could last over 75 rounds. The Queensberry rules introduced gloves, three-minute rounds and the 10-second knockout count — turning boxing from spectacle into a regulated sport.

questions.question: Why are the holes in a golf ball — the dimples — there at all?

answers.text: They reduce drag by triggering turbulent airflow, letting the ball fly further than a smooth one
They reduce the ball's weight so swing speeds can be higher
They were originally just decoration and were never proven to help

questions.fun_fact: Early players noticed scuffed old balls flew further than new smooth ones. Engineer William Taylor patented the dimple pattern in 1905. A typical dimpled ball travels roughly twice as far as a smooth one of the same weight.

questions.question: Tennis terminology — 'love' for zero — most likely derives from which root?

answers.text: The French 'l'oeuf' (the egg), because zero looks like an egg
The Old English 'lof' meaning praise
Cricket slang from the 1800s

questions.fun_fact: The 'egg' for nought theory parallels American baseball's 'goose egg' for zero. Some etymologists prefer 'playing for love' (playing for nothing), but the French connection is broadly accepted as the strongest match.

questions.question: Why does a standard ten-pin bowling lane have exactly 10 pins?

answers.text: To circumvent a 19th-century Connecticut law banning nine-pin bowling
It matches the number of digits on a player's hands
It was a marketing change to lift declining pub bowling revenue

questions.fun_fact: Connecticut banned nine-pin in 1841 because it was associated with gambling. Players added a tenth pin and rearranged them in a triangle — technically a different game, legally distinct, and the modern format stuck nationwide.

questions.question: The Tour de France's iconic yellow leader's jersey is yellow because of what?

answers.text: The newspaper L'Auto that organised it was printed on yellow paper
Yellow was the easiest colour for spectators to see at speed
The first leader insisted on his favourite colour

questions.fun_fact: The maillot jaune was introduced in 1919 to make the race leader visible in the peloton. L'Auto used yellow paper to stand out from its main rival, Le Vélo, which was green.

questions.question: Bo Jackson was a star in which two professional sports simultaneously?

answers.text: MLB baseball and NFL American football
NBA basketball and MLB baseball
NFL football and NHL ice hockey

questions.fun_fact: Jackson is the only athlete named an All-Star in both MLB and the NFL. A hip injury in a 1991 playoff game effectively ended both careers — he later played one more MLB season with a prosthetic hip.

questions.question: How long is a regulation Olympic swimming pool?

answers.text: 50 metres
100 metres
25 metres

questions.fun_fact: Short-course world records (25 m pools) are typically faster than long-course (50 m) records because each push-off the wall gives a brief speed boost. Many swimmers consider 25 m pools 'cheating fast'.

questions.question: What is the highest break possible in a single frame of snooker, under standard rules?
questions.fun_fact: The 147 'maximum' is the famous benchmark, but a free ball at the start can theoretically push it to 155. It has happened once in professional play: Jamie Burnett scored 148 in 2004.

questions.question: How many dimples does a standard regulation golf ball typically have?

answers.text: Between 300 and 500
Exactly 1,000
Around 50

questions.fun_fact: Most balls have 336 to 392 dimples in a precise geometric pattern. The exact number affects spin and flight; manufacturers fiercely guard their dimple geometries as trade secrets.

questions.question: Usain Bolt's 100m world record of 9.58 seconds was set in 2009. What was unusual about his reaction time at the start?

answers.text: It was 0.146 s — slower than several rivals he beat
It was the fastest ever recorded at 0.099 s
Officials initially disqualified him for a false start

questions.fun_fact: Bolt's top speed in that race reached over 44.7 km/h. His relatively slow starts and astonishing top-end were both due to his height (1.95 m) — taller frames take longer to accelerate but cover more ground per stride.

questions.question: What does a baseball umpire signal by sweeping both arms outward at waist level?

answers.text: Safe
Strike
Foul ball

questions.fun_fact: Hand signals were introduced in the late 19th century to help deaf player William Hoy follow the calls. They became permanent because they helped distant fans and players hear-impaired by stadium crowds.

questions.question: Why is a cricket Test match called a 'Test'?

answers.text: Because it tests the players' skill and stamina over five days
After a 19th-century cricket bat factory called Test Brothers
Because the first match was played on a ground named Test Field

questions.fun_fact: Test cricket began in 1877 between Australia and England. With sessions of about 6 hours daily for up to 5 days, a single match can run over 30 hours of play — the longest format in mainstream sport.

questions.question: The standard height of a basketball hoop has been 10 feet (3.05 m) since the sport was invented. Why?

answers.text: It's simply the height of the gymnasium balcony where Naismith first nailed up the peach baskets
It was set at the average reach of a tall man plus 50%
It was chosen at the 1936 Olympics as half the average court length

questions.fun_fact: Naismith nailed the baskets to the running track balcony in his Springfield, Massachusetts gymnasium. The balcony was 10 feet high. Despite players now averaging much taller than in 1891, the rim height has never been raised.

questions.question: Which rule did Formula 1 introduce in 2014 that often confused fans during a race?

answers.text: Double points awarded for the final race of the season
Mandatory pit stops every 15 laps
A reverse grid for the second race of a double-header

questions.fun_fact: The double-points rule was designed to keep championship suspense alive, but Lewis Hamilton clinched the 2014 title in Abu Dhabi anyway. The rule was so widely mocked that it was scrapped after just one season.

questions.question: What changed in figure skating scoring after the 2002 Salt Lake City judging scandal?

answers.text: The 6.0 system was scrapped for a cumulative points-based score with no maximum
Judges were forbidden from talking to each other during competition
Pairs skating was split into separate male and female events

questions.fun_fact: After a French judge admitted to a vote-swapping deal, the ISU replaced the iconic '6.0' system with a Code of Points where each element gets a base value plus 'grade of execution'. Theoretical maximums now run into the 300s for free skates.

questions.question: In professional sumo, what must the rikishi do at the very start of a bout before any pushing begins?

answers.text: Both wrestlers must place both fists on the clay at the same instant
Bow to the opponent without making eye contact for ten seconds
Throw a fistful of salt into the opponent's chest

questions.fun_fact: If the simultaneous touch (tachi-ai) is not synchronised, the gyoji halts the bout and orders a restart. Top wrestlers spend years studying their opponent's breathing rhythm to time the touch.

questions.question: Curling stones are made almost exclusively from granite quarried at only two places in the world. One is Wales. Where is the other?

answers.text: Ailsa Craig, a small uninhabited Scottish island
A quarry in northern Finland near Rovaniemi
A mine on Canada's Vancouver Island

questions.fun_fact: Ailsa Craig 'Blue Hone' granite is so dense it barely absorbs water, preventing the cracking that ruins lesser stones. Kays of Scotland holds exclusive harvesting rights and supplies almost every elite curling stone in the world.

questions.question: Why is a biathlon competitor penalised with a 150 m penalty loop for every shot they miss?

answers.text: Roughly the distance a top skier covers in the time a missed shot would have saved
It matches the historical distance between two Norwegian army outposts
It is the standard length of a Winter Olympic biathlon ski track

questions.fun_fact: The penalty was calibrated so that ski speed and shooting accuracy weigh roughly equally on the final time. In sprint events, one missed target can knock an athlete from gold contention to outside the top twenty.

questions.question: What is unusual about the playing surface of a hurling pitch compared with most field sports?

answers.text: It is one of the largest in team sport, up to 145 m long by 90 m wide
It must be cut on the diagonal so the grass leans toward the goal
It is required to slope by 2 percent toward one goalmouth

questions.fun_fact: An adult hurling pitch dwarfs a football field. Combined with the sliotar's speed of well over 150 km/h off the hurley, hurling is often described as the fastest field sport on grass.

questions.question: In cricket, what is a 'Nelson' and why are some players superstitious about it?

answers.text: A score of 111, considered unlucky in English cricket folklore
A delivery that bounces twice before reaching the batter
The position a fielder takes directly behind the umpire

questions.fun_fact: Umpire David Shepherd famously hopped on one leg whenever the score reached 111, 222 or any multiple, to ward off the curse. The origin is said to relate to Admiral Nelson reputedly having 'one eye, one arm, one' — though that detail is mostly myth.

questions.question: Why does the America's Cup yacht race use boats designed specifically for each edition rather than a standard class?

answers.text: The defender chooses the boat type and rules, a tradition baked into the Deed of Gift
Modern carbon hulls warp after one season and cannot be reused
Race organisers auction the design rights to the highest sponsor every cycle

questions.fun_fact: The defender's right to pick the venue, schedule and class has produced wild swings — from massive J-class sloops in the 1930s to today's foiling catamarans that fly above the water at over 90 km/h.

questions.question: What did the introduction of the offside rule change in early association football?

answers.text: It ended the era of forwards permanently camped near the opponent's goal
It allowed goalkeepers to handle the ball outside the penalty area
It made throw-ins legal for the first time

questions.fun_fact: Before the rule, attackers stood by the opposing keeper waiting for long boots forward. The 1925 reform — needing only two defenders between attacker and goal instead of three — caused goals per game to nearly double in one season.

questions.question: The first international football match in 1872 between Scotland and England ended with what score?

answers.text: 4-2 to Scotland
3-1 to England

questions.fun_fact: Played in Glasgow before 4,000 spectators, the match was goalless partly because both teams used radically different formations — England with seven forwards, Scotland with a then-revolutionary passing game using only six.

questions.question: What is the only Olympic medal made from material recovered from electronic waste?

answers.text: Every medal at Tokyo 2020
Only the gold medal at Beijing 2022
The bronze medals at Rio 2016

questions.fun_fact: Japan ran a two-year national drive collecting old smartphones and small appliances, yielding about 32 kg of gold, 3,500 kg of silver and 2,200 kg of bronze — enough to mint all 5,000 medals from recycled metals.

questions.question: Why do speed skaters wear skin-tight suits with a small hood that covers their hair?

answers.text: Loose hair creates measurable aerodynamic drag at speeds above 50 km/h
International rules require the head to be fully covered for safety
Body heat retention via the scalp prevents leg cramps

questions.fun_fact: Wind-tunnel tests at the Dutch national team showed even a few centimetres of exposed hair could cost an athlete 0.1 seconds over 500 m — enough to flip a podium finish.

questions.question: In Formula 1, what does the chequered flag at the finish line actually signify under the regulations?

answers.text: The end of the race, with positions frozen as cars cross the line for the final time
A warning that the leader has one lap remaining
An optional rest lap before the official end of the session

questions.fun_fact: The chequered flag's origin is disputed but the earliest documented use is from a 1906 French race. Pre-radio, the bold black-and-white pattern was simply the most visible signal a marshal could wave at a passing car.

questions.question: Why is the marathon almost always the final event on the athletics programme at the Olympic Games?

answers.text: Tradition since 1896 places it as the symbolic closing event of the Games
It is the only race that requires the city's streets to be closed
Television networks insisted on a guaranteed prime-time finale

questions.fun_fact: At several Games the marathon finishers actually run their final metres inside the closing ceremony, with medals presented in front of the full stadium crowd — a deliberate echo of the legend of Pheidippides.

questions.question: What unusual physical adaptation do elite freedivers train to slow their oxygen use underwater?

answers.text: Triggering the mammalian dive reflex, which lowers heart rate and constricts blood vessels
Voluntarily reducing red blood cell count before competition
Inhaling pure helium to reduce metabolic load

questions.fun_fact: The dive reflex is present in all humans but stronger in trained freedivers — some can drop their pulse from 70 to under 30 beats per minute within seconds of facial contact with cold water.

questions.question: What does the term 'peloton' literally mean in the Tour de France?

answers.text: A 'little ball' or platoon — the main bunch of riders moving together
The lone breakaway leader at the front of the race
A team's designated sprinter for the day's stage

questions.fun_fact: Riders at the back of a large peloton expend up to 40 percent less energy than the leader thanks to the slipstream — a fact that shapes nearly every tactical decision in road cycling.

questions.question: What is the official maximum height a sumo wrestler may have his hair styled into for top-division bouts?

answers.text: There is no height limit, but only top-division rikishi wear the ginkgo-leaf oicho-mage
Exactly 10 cm above the crown of the head
Half the wrestler's neck circumference

questions.fun_fact: The oicho-mage takes a specialised stablehand called a tokoyama up to 20 minutes to arrange. When a wrestler retires, his topknot is ceremonially cut piece by piece by friends, family and finally his coach.

questions.question: What is unusual about the trophy awarded to the FA Cup winners in English football?

answers.text: The current trophy is the fourth design used since 1872
It is solid gold and weighs over 12 kilograms
It is the same physical trophy that was awarded in 1872

questions.fun_fact: The original was stolen from a Birmingham shop window in 1895 and never recovered — likely melted down for the silver. A second version was retired in 1910, a third served from 1911 to 1991, and the current replica is in everyday use.

questions.question: Which marker on a tennis court is sometimes nicknamed the 'tramlines'?

answers.text: The pair of parallel lines down each side, used only for doubles
The baseline and service line viewed from the umpire's chair
The two service boxes when seen end-on

questions.fun_fact: The tramlines widen the court for doubles but are out of bounds in singles. The court width difference is 1.37 m on each side — a deceptively large area that completely changes serve angles.

questions.question: Why does an ice hockey rink have rounded corners rather than square ones?

answers.text: To let the puck flow continuously around the boards without dead spots
Square corners caused the ice to crack along the joins
Goalkeepers historically lobbied for a smaller defensive zone

questions.fun_fact: The original rinks were rectangular fields used for outdoor pond hockey, where corners drifted naturally with the ice. The first indoor rink to use deliberately rounded corners was Montreal's Victoria Skating Rink in 1875.

questions.question: What forced FIFA to introduce goal-line technology in 2014?

answers.text: A Frank Lampard shot in 2010 that crossed the line but was not given as a goal
Repeated controversies in the South American qualifiers of 2013
A petition signed by every UEFA referee that year

questions.fun_fact: Lampard's shot for England against Germany at the 2010 World Cup struck the bar, bounced over the line by nearly a metre, and was waved away. FIFA president Sepp Blatter, who had long opposed the technology, publicly reversed course within days.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the small hole on a bowling ball besides the three finger holes?

answers.text: It is a balance hole drilled to fine-tune the ball's rotation
It vents heat generated by friction with the lane
It is purely decorative and identifies the manufacturer

questions.fun_fact: Balance holes were so effective at letting bowlers tweak the ball's reaction that the US Bowling Congress banned them in 2020. Top-level players had to relearn their hook with cleanly drilled finger holes only.

questions.question: Why are professional rugby balls oval rather than round?

answers.text: The original pig-bladder ball took an oval shape when inflated
World Rugby chose the shape in 1923 to differentiate from football
Oval balls were proven more aerodynamic by 19th-century physicists

questions.fun_fact: Early balls used inflated pig bladders inside leather, which naturally bulged longer than wide. Once rubber bladders arrived in the 1870s, makers could have chosen any shape — but by then the oval had defined the sport.

questions.question: In which sport would you legitimately attempt a 'Phelps' turn?

answers.text: Competitive swimming butterfly
Synchronised diving
Water polo

questions.fun_fact: The 'Phelps' is a slang term for an open turn done so quickly the swimmer barely loses momentum. Michael Phelps's turn times in the 200 m butterfly were routinely a tenth of a second faster than his nearest rival's.

questions.question: Why are golf courses traditionally laid out with exactly 18 holes?

answers.text: St Andrews settled on 18 in 1764 and the rest of the world copied it
It matches the average number of strokes a beginner takes per hole
Eighteen was chosen by the R&A to fit a four-hour round of play

questions.fun_fact: The Old Course originally had 22 holes; players reduced it to 18 by combining short ones in 1764. Because St Andrews was already the most prestigious club, the new layout became the global standard within a generation.

questions.question: What is the legal status of icing the puck in ice hockey?

answers.text: It is a violation that stops play and forces a face-off in the offending team's zone
It is a strategic option that costs the team a two-minute minor penalty
It is allowed only when the team is shorthanded

questions.fun_fact: Icing — clearing the puck from your own half across the opposing goal line untouched — was banned in 1937 after a New York Americans game in which Boston iced the puck more than 60 times to protect a 3-2 lead.

questions.question: Why do elite marathon runners often wear shoes with a thick foam midsole and an embedded carbon fibre plate?

answers.text: The plate stiffens the shoe and stores elastic energy, returning a measurable percentage on each stride
The plate is purely cosmetic and was introduced as a marketing gimmick
The plate prevents stress fractures by limiting foot flex

questions.fun_fact: Independent biomechanics studies found the technology improves running economy by around 4 percent — enough that World Athletics now caps midsole stack height at 40 mm to prevent shoe technology from rewriting record books overnight.

questions.question: What is the lowest possible numerical score with which a darts player can finish a leg in a standard 501 game?

answers.text: Two, with a double-one finish
Zero, by hitting any bullseye twice in a row
Three, by hitting triple-one

questions.fun_fact: The 501 game requires you to end on a double. The smallest legal checkout is therefore a single double-one. The most prestigious finish is the nine-darter: scoring 501 in the minimum possible nine throws.

questions.question: What is the role of the 'libero' in indoor volleyball?

answers.text: A specialist back-row defender who wears a different-coloured shirt
The team captain who must remain at the net at all times
A roaming player allowed to spike from anywhere on the court

questions.fun_fact: The libero was introduced in 1998 to extend rallies after teams complained that booming serves were ending matches too quickly. They cannot attack the ball above net height and cannot serve in most international competitions.

questions.question: Why is a free kick called 'indirect' in football?

answers.text: Another player must touch the ball before it can legally enter the goal
The kick must be aimed away from the goal as a courtesy
The referee must touch the ball before it is kicked

questions.fun_fact: Referees signal an indirect free kick by holding one arm vertically in the air until the kick is taken and a second player touches the ball. Goals scored directly from an indirect free kick are disallowed and result in a goal kick to the opposition.

questions.question: What unusual hazard sometimes interrupts play at Augusta National during the Masters golf tournament?

answers.text: Tree pollen so dense it visibly drifts across the fairways
Migrating monarch butterflies that settle on the greens
Sudden subsidence of greens due to underlying sinkholes

questions.fun_fact: Augusta sits in one of the US's pollen-heaviest cities each April. Players have described seeing visible yellow clouds when they hit out of trees, and several have withdrawn over allergic reactions.

questions.question: Why is the goal in lacrosse much smaller than in football, despite the ball being smaller?

answers.text: The goal is sized so a goalkeeper with a stick can plausibly cover most of it
It was scaled down from a 19th-century football goal by exactly one-third
It is made smaller to fit indoor box lacrosse arenas

questions.fun_fact: The men's lacrosse goal is a 6-foot square. Shots regularly exceed 160 km/h, so even covering a goal that small with an oversized stick gives the goalkeeper only fractions of a second to react.

questions.question: What is the standard surface of a Wimbledon tennis court?

answers.text: 100 percent perennial ryegrass
Synthetic grass over a rubber base
A blend of ryegrass and clay particles

questions.fun_fact: Wimbledon switched to pure ryegrass in 2001 for durability. Each court is mown to exactly 8 mm during the Championships, and the centre courts are reseeded every September and shut to play until the following June.

questions.question: What does the 'pursuit' format in cross-country skiing mean for the starting order?

answers.text: Skiers start at staggered intervals based on the time gaps from a previous race
All skiers start together but must follow the leader for the first kilometre
Skiers race in pairs, hunting down the pair ahead of them

questions.fun_fact: Pursuit racing means the first skier across the line is genuinely the day's winner — no need to wait for time calculations. The format also tends to produce dramatic late-race chases that work well on television.

questions.question: Why do high jumpers approach the bar from a curved run-up rather than a straight one?

answers.text: The curve generates centripetal lean, lowering the jumper's centre of mass at takeoff
It is required by World Athletics to standardise approach angles
A straight run-up was banned after multiple bar-clearing controversies

questions.fun_fact: Dick Fosbury revolutionised the event in 1968 with the back-first 'Fosbury Flop', which only works with a curved approach. Within a decade, almost every elite jumper had switched, and earlier styles like the straddle vanished from top competition.

questions.question: Which event was added to the Winter Olympics in 1998 specifically to attract younger viewers?

answers.text: Snowboarding
Freestyle aerials skiing
Short-track speed skating

questions.fun_fact: Snowboarding debuted at Nagano with halfpipe and giant slalom. The first gold medallist, Canadian Ross Rebagliati, briefly lost it to a positive cannabis test before the IOC ruled the substance was not on the banned list at the time.

questions.question: What is unusual about the orientation of a baseball home plate compared with the other three bases?

answers.text: It is a five-sided pentagon while the others are square
It is raised slightly above the level of the pitcher's mound
It is made of leather rather than rubber or stone

questions.fun_fact: Home plate was originally a 12-inch square, but umpires struggled to judge balls and strikes over a flat front edge. In 1900 a point was added facing the catcher, giving the plate its now-iconic pentagonal shape.

questions.question: Why do professional cyclists shave their legs?

answers.text: Mainly for easier post-crash wound cleaning and massage, not aerodynamics
Hair adds measurable wind resistance at racing speeds
Shaved legs help skin sweat evaporate faster during climbs

questions.fun_fact: Wind-tunnel tests show shaved legs do save a tiny amount of drag at race speeds — about 5 watts over an hour — but riders and team doctors agree the real benefit is keeping road rash clean and bandageable.

questions.question: Why does an outdoor 400 m running track have staggered starting lines for sprint events?

answers.text: Outer lanes are longer around the curve, so starts are offset to equalise distance
It prevents runners from drafting in each other's slipstream
It reduces wind interference from competitors ahead

questions.fun_fact: The radius of the outermost lane on a standard track is roughly 7 metres greater than the innermost. Across a full 400 m lap, that adds up to about 53 metres extra running — corrected entirely by the staggered start.

questions.question: What is the name of the lane in cricket between the two sets of stumps?

answers.text: The pitch
The crease
The runway

questions.fun_fact: A Test pitch is 22 yards long — a length set in 1744 to match the historical English measurement of a 'chain'. Groundskeepers spend days preparing each pitch's surface to favour batters, bowlers or a balanced contest.

questions.question: Which luge event was added to the Winter Olympics programme at Sochi 2014, bringing the total to four?

answers.text: Team relay
Mixed doubles
Sprint singles

questions.fun_fact: The relay involves a man, a woman and a doubles pair sliding in sequence, each triggering a touchpad to start the next. Germany dominated the format in its first three Games, winning every gold medal between 2014 and 2022.

questions.question: Why is a typical professional cycling team built around a single 'general classification' rider rather than every rider racing for themselves?

answers.text: Drafting and tactical sacrifice mean a protected leader can finish minutes ahead of solo rivals
UCI rules require teams to nominate a single leader before each Grand Tour
Sponsors pay bonuses only when one rider wins the overall classification

questions.fun_fact: Teammates donate wheels, shelter the leader from the wind, and even sacrifice their own bikes during mechanical failures. A typical Tour de France winner spends roughly 80 percent of riding time tucked safely inside the team's protective formation.

questions.question: Why does a clay tennis court visibly affect ball behaviour compared with grass?

answers.text: The crushed brick surface grips the ball, slowing it and increasing its bounce height
Clay absorbs spin entirely, making slice serves ineffective
Clay reflects more heat, softening the ball over a long match

questions.fun_fact: The slower bounce favours grinding baseliners and is why Rafael Nadal won the French Open 14 times — more than any player has won any other single Grand Slam.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of players a football team may have on the pitch at one time?

answers.text: Eleven, including the goalkeeper
Ten outfield players plus the goalkeeper, for twelve total
Nine in normal play, with substitutes adding two more

questions.fun_fact: If a team drops below seven players — through red cards or injuries with no substitutes left — the match is automatically abandoned. This has happened repeatedly in lower-league football, most famously when Sheffield United were reduced to six against West Brom in 2002.

questions.question: Why does the heart rate of a Tour de France climber spike well above what cardiologists consider safe at rest?

answers.text: Trained endurance hearts can sustain rates of 180+ for hours without harm thanks to a hugely enlarged stroke volume
Climbers deliberately enter cardiac arrhythmia to boost short-term power
Tour doctors permit temporary use of stimulants on mountain stages

questions.fun_fact: An elite climber's resting heart rate may be in the 30s while their maximum reaches the high 190s. Stroke volume — blood pumped per beat — is often twice that of a sedentary adult, letting the heart move enormous oxygen loads.

questions.question: What is the function of the small 'dimpled' surface on the grip end of a tennis racquet?

answers.text: It gives the overgrip something to bond with so it does not rotate during play
It absorbs vibration from off-centre hits
It allows umpires to identify the player's racquet brand from a distance

questions.fun_fact: Most pros wrap a fresh overgrip every match or two; the textured base layer is what keeps the new grip from sliding when their hands get sweaty during long rallies.

questions.question: Why did the modern pentathlon, designed by Pierre de Coubertin, include the specific events of pistol shooting, fencing, swimming, riding and running?

answers.text: They were the imagined skills of a 19th-century cavalry officer caught behind enemy lines
Each event represents a different ancient Greek god
They were chosen by lot from Coubertin's favourite sports

questions.fun_fact: Coubertin envisioned a soldier shooting his way out, fencing past a guard, swimming a river, riding an unfamiliar horse and running home. The riding event uses an unfamiliar horse drawn by lot — a deliberate echo of the original premise.

questions.question: Why are footballs in a stadium often kept inside a heated cabinet during cold-weather matches?

answers.text: Cold air inside the ball reduces pressure, making it fly differently and feel sluggish
Cold leather absorbs water that freezes in mid-air
Stadium rules ban balls below a fixed temperature for safety

questions.fun_fact: A drop of 10 °C lowers a ball's internal pressure by roughly 0.4 psi. The NFL's 2015 'Deflategate' controversy was eventually explained partly by this effect — though investigators disagreed about how much was deliberate.

questions.question: What does a baseball pitcher's 'splitter' grip do to the ball's flight path?

answers.text: It causes the ball to suddenly drop downward late in its trajectory
It makes the ball curve gently sideways like a slider
It accelerates the ball over the final five metres

questions.fun_fact: The fingers split widely across the seams produce reduced backspin compared with a fastball, so gravity wins out faster than batters expect. Pitchers blame the splitter for the high elbow-injury rates seen in 1980s and 90s pitchers.

questions.question: Which footballing role did the 'false nine' famously revive in the 2010s?

answers.text: A nominal centre-forward who drops deep, dragging defenders out of position
A goalkeeper who plays outfield in the final minutes
A defender allowed to score from open play only

questions.fun_fact: Pep Guardiola used Lionel Messi as a false nine for Barcelona, creating empty central space for wide players to attack. The tactic so disorganised opponents that it shaped a decade of midfield-heavy formations across Europe.

questions.question: What is the role of a 'pacemaker' in elite middle-distance and long-distance track racing?

answers.text: A runner hired to set a fast pre-agreed pace for the first portion of the race
A device worn on the wrist that flashes the target lap time
The lead athlete in a championship final by reputation

questions.fun_fact: Pacemakers — sometimes called rabbits — drop out partway through, having helped set up a fast time. They are common in record-attempt meets but banned from championship finals, where tactical racing rules the day.

questions.question: Why is the strike zone in baseball defined relative to the batter's body rather than a fixed height?

answers.text: Tall and short batters would otherwise have wildly different effective hitting zones
Catchers historically lobbied for an adjustable zone to ease their reach
Pitchers used to grip the ball to a fixed height before each pitch

questions.fun_fact: The current rule defines the zone from the midpoint between the shoulders and the top of the trousers down to the hollow beneath the kneecap. Automated strike-zone tracking now triangulates each batter's exact dimensions before every at-bat.

questions.question: Why does the discus thrower spin before releasing the discus rather than throwing from a standing position?

answers.text: The rotation adds tangential velocity, dramatically increasing release speed
Standing throws are explicitly banned by World Athletics rules
The spin lets the thrower align the discus with the prevailing wind

questions.fun_fact: Top throwers complete one and a half turns in around 1.5 seconds, reaching release speeds of 25 m/s or more. A standing throw of the same discus typically travels less than half the distance of a rotational throw.

questions.question: Why are short-track speed-skating helmets often equipped with a chin strap that can break away under load?

answers.text: A breakaway strap prevents neck injury if the helmet snags during a high-speed crash
It allows officials to remove the helmet quickly during medal ceremonies
The strap doubles as a microphone mount for coaches

questions.fun_fact: Short-track crashes routinely send multiple skaters sliding into the padded barriers at over 50 km/h. A helmet that detaches cleanly under sudden force is considered safer than one that pulls the skater's head backward.

questions.question: Why does a curveball in baseball actually curve, according to physicists?

answers.text: The spin makes air move faster on one side, lowering pressure and pushing the ball sideways
The ball's stitches catch crosswinds that physically blow it off course
The ball deforms in flight and rolls toward its heavier side

questions.fun_fact: This is the Magnus effect. The break looks like a sharp last-second jerk, but high-speed cameras show the curve is actually a smooth, continuous arc the whole way to the plate — the 'break' is an illusion of the batter's perspective.

questions.question: What happens inside a sprinter's muscles in the final metres of a 100 m race that forces even the fastest runners to slow down?

answers.text: Their fuel system can't resupply fast enough, so power output drops before the finish
Lactic acid physically dissolves the muscle fibres mid-stride
The lungs run completely out of stored oxygen at exactly 80 metres

questions.fun_fact: Top sprinters actually reach peak speed around 60-70 m and then decelerate slightly to the line. The 100 m is won not by who accelerates most but by who slows down least — phosphocreatine stores in the muscle empty in roughly 8-10 seconds.

questions.question: Why can a skilled archer's heartbeat ruin a shot, and what do they do about it?

answers.text: They release the arrow in the gap between heartbeats to avoid the pulse jolting the bow
They hold their breath until the heart temporarily stops
They press the bow against the chest so the heartbeat steadies the aim

questions.fun_fact: Each heartbeat sends a tiny tremor up the arm that can shift the aim point. Elite archers and biathletes train to feel their pulse and squeeze the release in the roughly half-second lull between beats.

questions.question: Why do swimmers exhale underwater instead of holding their breath the whole stroke cycle?

answers.text: Holding air makes them too buoyant and creates tension, so steady exhaling keeps the body level and relaxed
Exhaling underwater cools the lungs and prevents overheating
The rules forbid surfacing with air still in the lungs

questions.fun_fact: A chest full of held air floats the upper body and sinks the legs, wrecking the streamlined position. Continuous exhalation also means the swimmer only needs a quick inhale when the mouth clears the water, costing less time.

questions.question: Why does chalk help a gymnast or weightlifter grip the bar better?

answers.text: It absorbs sweat and moisture, so the skin grips the bar instead of sliding on a film of water
It chemically softens the skin so it moulds around the bar
It creates a sticky glue-like layer between hand and metal

questions.fun_fact: Gym chalk is magnesium carbonate, not the calcium chalk used on blackboards. Counter-intuitively, it works by drying the skin rather than adding stickiness — friction between dry skin and bar is far higher than between wet skin and bar.

questions.question: Why is it physically impossible to keep your eye fully on the ball at the moment you hit it in fast sports like tennis or baseball?

answers.text: The ball moves faster than the eye can track in the final fraction of a second, so the brain predicts where it will be
Blinking is an involuntary reflex that always triggers on contact
The eye loses focus whenever the head turns toward the ball

questions.fun_fact: Eye-tracking studies show batters lose sight of a fast pitch several metres before contact. 'Keep your eye on the ball' is impossible to obey literally — what good hitters actually do is jump their gaze ahead to the predicted contact point.

questions.question: Why does a footballer's free kick suddenly 'dip' or swerve more violently when struck a certain way?

answers.text: At a critical speed the airflow around the ball changes from smooth to turbulent, abruptly altering the forces on it
The ball heats up from the impact and the warm air inside makes it lighter
Stadium air pressure changes when the crowd inhales together

questions.fun_fact: The famous 'knuckleball' free kick is struck with almost no spin near this transition speed, so the airflow flips erratically and the ball wobbles unpredictably. A ball with smoother panels reaches the chaotic zone at a different speed, which is why new World Cup balls spark goalkeeper complaints.

questions.question: Why do cross-country skiers apply a different wax to the middle of the ski than to the tips and tails?

answers.text: The middle 'grip' wax holds the snow for push-off, while the ends are slick so the ski glides forward
The middle wax is purely to protect the ski from the skier's weight
Coloured middle wax helps judges identify each skier from a distance

questions.fun_fact: When a classic skier presses down, the ski's camber flattens and the grip wax bites the snow to push off; when they glide, the camber lifts the grip zone clear so only the slick ends touch. Getting the wax wrong for the day's snow temperature can lose a race outright.

questions.question: Why does spinning rapidly let a figure skater pull their arms in and suddenly whirl faster?

answers.text: Pulling mass closer to the spin axis conserves rotation, so the same energy spins them faster
Tucked arms reduce air resistance against the body
The skate blade grips the ice more when the body is compact

questions.fun_fact: This is conservation of angular momentum — the same physics that makes a collapsing star spin up. A skater can roughly double their spin rate just by drawing the arms and a leg into the body, with no extra push from the ice.

questions.question: Why do boxers exhale sharply with a hiss every time they throw a punch?

answers.text: Tensing the core on a sharp exhale braces the body so more force transfers into the punch
It cools the blood rushing to the arms
It is purely to intimidate the opponent with the sound

questions.fun_fact: The forced exhale stiffens the trunk so the punching arm has a solid base to drive from, and it also empties the lungs so a body shot landing at that instant does less damage. The same breath-and-brace trick appears in martial arts as the 'kiai' shout.

questions.question: Why does a basketball player's jump shot fly truer with backspin on the ball?

answers.text: Backspin makes the ball deflect softly off the rim and gives it a more stable, predictable flight
Backspin makes the ball lighter as it rises
Backspin magnetises the ball slightly toward the metal rim

questions.fun_fact: A backspinning shot that hits the rim tends to grab and drop in rather than bounce away, giving 'shooter's roll'. The spin also lends the ball a steadier, more consistent flight through the air.

questions.question: Why does a long jumper run a long approach before takeoff instead of jumping from a standing start?

answers.text: Forward running speed is converted into horizontal distance, so faster approach means a longer jump
The run-up is needed to memorise the exact takeoff foot
Rules require a minimum approach distance of 30 metres

questions.fun_fact: Roughly the same fast athletes win both the long jump and the sprints, because horizontal speed at the board is the single biggest factor in distance. Standing long jump exists as a separate event and produces less than half the distance of a running jump.

questions.question: Why does a tennis ball bounce lower and slower as a match wears on?

answers.text: Repeated impacts fluff up the felt and let pressurised air slowly leak out, deadening the bounce
The ball absorbs sweat and becomes heavier
Friction permanently flattens one side of the rubber core

questions.fun_fact: Pressurised tennis balls start losing air the moment the can is opened, which is why pros demand fresh balls every nine games. The roughened, fluffed felt also creates more drag, slowing the ball through the air as well as off the court.

questions.question: Why do downhill speed skiers crouch into an extreme tuck rather than standing tall for better balance?

answers.text: The tuck slashes air resistance, which is by far the biggest force slowing them at high speed
Crouching lets the skis carve deeper into the snow for grip
The low position keeps blood from rushing to the head

questions.fun_fact: At over 130 km/h, air resistance dwarfs the friction of skis on snow. Wind-tunnel work on the tuck position can be worth several km/h, which over a long course is the difference between a medal and mid-pack.

questions.question: Why does a properly thrown javelin briefly point slightly upward as it flies, then level off?

answers.text: It is launched nose-high so it slices into the air efficiently and glides like a small wing
The metal tip is heated before throwing to make it rise
Air trapped in the hollow shaft lifts the front

questions.fun_fact: The javelin is a gliding airfoil, and its balance point matters enormously. The men's javelin was actually redesigned in 1986 to move the centre of gravity forward, making it nosedive sooner — throws had grown so long that javelins were nearly reaching the far end of stadiums.

questions.question: Why do elite runners breathe in a rhythm linked to their footsteps?

answers.text: Coordinating breath with stride reduces strain from the impact forces hitting the body each step
It is required by the body's inability to breathe and move legs at once
Matched rhythm sends more blood to the lungs than to the legs

questions.fun_fact: Many runners settle into a 2:2 pattern — inhale for two steps, exhale for two. Exhaling always lands on the same foot, so some coaches teach alternating patterns like 3:2 to spread the landing stress evenly between both legs and reduce side stitches.

questions.question: Why does cold water make a freediver's body involuntarily slow its heart rate?

answers.text: Cold on the face triggers a built-in reflex that conserves oxygen for the brain and heart
Cold water thickens the blood so the heart pumps less often
The cold numbs the nerves that signal the heart to beat

questions.fun_fact: Just splashing cold water on your face triggers a milder version of this same reflex — your pulse drops within seconds. It is shared with diving mammals like seals, and is strongest when the water is cold and the breath is held together.

questions.question: Why does a cyclist riding closely behind another save a large amount of energy?

answers.text: The lead rider punches a hole in the air, leaving a low-pressure pocket the follower coasts into
The follower is pulled forward by the lead rider's tyre suction on the road
Two bikes close together weigh less due to combined momentum

questions.fun_fact: At racing speed most of a cyclist's effort goes to pushing air aside, so tucking into the slipstream can cut energy use by around a third. This is why breakaway riders, alone in the wind, are so often reeled in by a sheltered chasing pack.

questions.question: Why does a golfer's drive travel farther on a hot day than a cold one, all else being equal?

answers.text: Warm air is less dense, so the ball meets less resistance and flies farther
Heat makes the golf ball expand and become more aerodynamic
Warm muscles always swing exactly 10 percent faster

questions.fun_fact: Thinner warm air means less drag but also slightly less lift, yet the distance gain still wins out — roughly a couple of yards per 10°C. This is also why drives go dramatically farther at high altitude, where the air is thinner still.

questions.question: Why do sprinters explode out of a crouched start in blocks rather than starting upright?

answers.text: The forward lean lets them push against the blocks and drive the body's weight into acceleration
Crouching stores energy in the spine like a spring
The low start hides the runner's eyes from the starting gun's flash

questions.fun_fact: Blocks give something solid to push against, and the low body angle means more of the leg drive goes into forward motion rather than straight up. Runners stay leaning forward for the first several strides, only standing tall once near top speed.

questions.question: Why does a ski jumper hold the skis in a wide 'V' shape in the air instead of keeping them parallel?

answers.text: The V spreads more surface to the oncoming air, generating extra lift to fly farther
The V keeps the skis from crossing and tripping the jumper
Parallel skis are banned for being too dangerous on landing

questions.fun_fact: The V-style was mocked when Sweden's Jan Boklov adopted it in the late 1980s and judges docked his style points — but he won so much on distance that everyone copied it. It generates noticeably more lift than the old parallel-ski technique.

questions.question: Why does a weightlifter often perform better when chalk-coated and breathing in just before a heavy lift?

answers.text: Holding a deep breath pressurises the abdomen, creating a rigid core that protects the spine and transfers force
The held breath floods the muscles with extra stored oxygen
Inhaling makes the body lighter against gravity

questions.fun_fact: This braced breath-hold is the Valsalva manoeuvre, and it turns the torso into a stiff column that stops the lifter folding under the bar. Doing it on every rep does spike blood pressure sharply, which is why it is reserved for genuinely heavy efforts.

questions.question: Why does a thrown discus travel farther when it tilts slightly into a headwind?

answers.text: Like a wing, it generates more lift flying into the wind, which keeps it airborne longer
The headwind cools the metal and reduces its weight
Wind from the front spins the discus faster, adding distance

questions.fun_fact: Counter to intuition, a discus can fly farther into a moderate headwind than with a tailwind, because the faster airflow over its angled face produces more lift. Throwers actively read the flag and time their attempts for the right breeze.

questions.question: Why do speed skaters' clap skates have a hinge that lets the blade detach from the heel during each stride?

answers.text: The hinge keeps the blade flat on the ice longer, letting the skater push for more of each stride
The hinge folds the skate flat for easier carrying
It lets skaters quickly swap blades between races

questions.fun_fact: In a fixed skate, lifting the heel pulls the blade tip off the ice and ends the push early. The hinged clap skate, which snaps back with an audible clap, keeps the blade down through the full ankle extension — it cut world records dramatically when introduced in the late 1990s.

questions.question: The word 'soccer' is actually an abbreviation of which longer term?

answers.text: Association football
Society football
Scottish football

questions.fun_fact: British students in the 1880s shortened 'Association' to 'assoc' and then 'soccer', the same slang habit that turned 'rugby' fans into 'ruggers'. The term was common in England long before Americans adopted it.

questions.question: What gave the sport of badminton its name?

answers.text: It was named after Badminton House, an English country estate
It comes from the Sanskrit word for shuttlecock
It was named after the British India town of Badminton

questions.fun_fact: Guests of the Duke of Beaufort played an Indian game called 'poona' in the great hall of Badminton House in Gloucestershire around 1873. The estate's name simply stuck to the game they brought back.

questions.question: The marathon-style event of the 'pentathlon' aside, which modern Olympic sport takes its name from a Greek word meaning 'feat of strength'?

answers.text: Athletics, from 'athlon' (prize/contest)
Gymnastics, from 'gymnos' (strength)
Decathlon, from 'deka-thlon' (strong ten)

questions.fun_fact: 'Athlon' meant a contest fought for a prize, and an 'athletes' was one who competed for it. The root reveals that prize-winning, not mere participation, was baked into the very word from the start.

questions.question: Why is the scoring system in tennis based on the unusual sequence 15, 30, 40?

answers.text: It likely came from a clock face, with points marked at quarter-hour positions
It was copied from the points in a French dice game
It reflects the original betting stakes of 15, 30 and 40 sous

questions.fun_fact: The clock-face theory holds that 45 was shortened to 40 so the hand could move to 50 for the 'advantage' before reaching 60 for game. No single record proves it, but the quarter-hour pattern fits remarkably well.

questions.question: The word 'gymnasium' comes from a Greek practice that would scandalise a modern gym. What did 'gymnos' mean?

answers.text: Naked
Sweating
Disciplined

questions.fun_fact: Greek athletes trained and competed nude, and a 'gymnasion' was literally 'a place to be naked'. The modern word for a school subject and a fitness centre still carries that root, minus the dress code.

questions.question: The game of squash got its name from what physical property of its ball?

answers.text: The ball squashes against the wall on impact
Players were squashed together in a small court
It was first played with a squashed tennis ball

questions.fun_fact: Squash evolved at Harrow School around 1830 when boys used a punctured, softer rackets ball that 'squashed' on the wall instead of bouncing hard. The squashy ball demanded more running, which is exactly why the game caught on.

questions.question: The card game term aside, why is the at-bat hitting area in baseball called the 'batter's box'?

answers.text: It was added to stop batters creeping forward toward the pitcher
Early batters stood inside an actual wooden crate
It marks where the equipment box once sat

questions.fun_fact: Before the box was drawn, hitters would edge closer to the plate to attack pitches early. The chalk rectangle, formalised in the 1870s, fixed the batter's legal standing area and the rule survives essentially unchanged.

questions.question: Why does golf use the term 'caddie' for the person carrying a player's clubs?

answers.text: From the French 'cadet', meaning a young helper or junior
From a Scottish word for a leather club bag
From the surname of golf's first professional club-carrier

questions.fun_fact: Mary, Queen of Scots, who learned golf in France, is said to have used military 'cadets' to carry her clubs. The word entered Scots as 'cawdy' for an errand boy before settling on the golf course.

questions.question: The word 'derby' for a local sporting rivalry traces back to which original event?

answers.text: A chaotic mass football game between two parishes in Derby, England
The Earl of Derby's private fencing tournaments
A 19th-century Derby cricket club's grudge matches

questions.fun_fact: Shrovetide football in Derby pitted two halves of the town against each other in a violent, day-long scrum. 'Local derby' came to mean any heated neighbourhood contest, and the horse race at Epsom borrowed the name separately from the Earl of Derby.

questions.question: What is the original purpose of the 'pea' inside a football referee's whistle?

answers.text: The rattling pea makes the trilling sound that carries over a crowd
It marks whistles approved for international matches
It lets the referee taste-test for tampering

questions.fun_fact: Whistles were invented by Joseph Hudson of Birmingham, who first sold them to London police. His pea whistle, the Acme Thunderer, launched in 1884 and its loud, carrying trill let referees finally be heard above the roar of the crowd.

questions.question: The boxing term 'southpaw' for a left-handed fighter is popularly said to have borrowed its name from which other sport?

answers.text: Baseball
Cricket
Fencing

questions.fun_fact: According to the popular story, early American ballparks were oriented so a left-handed pitcher's throwing arm faced south, and sportswriters dubbed him a 'southpaw'. Boxing later adopted the word for left-handers, though lexicographers note the term may actually predate the game.

questions.question: Why is the long-distance running event called a 'marathon' rather than being named after a runner?

answers.text: It honours a messenger's legendary run from the town of Marathon
'Marathon' was ancient Greek for 'great endurance'
It was named after the Marathon family who funded the first race

questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the place, not the man. The runner Pheidippides supposedly carried news of victory from the plain of Marathon to Athens, and the 1896 organisers named the new race after his route's starting point.

questions.question: The word 'rugby' came about because of an incident at Rugby School involving which act?

answers.text: A boy picked up the ball and ran with it during football
A headmaster banned a rougher ball game and renamed it
Students invented an oval ball in the school workshop

questions.fun_fact: The legend credits pupil William Webb Ellis with first running while carrying the ball around 1823. Historians doubt the exact tale, but the school's distinctive handling game spread under the town's name, and rugby's World Cup trophy is named the Webb Ellis Cup.

questions.question: Why does the sport of curling refer to its playing area as a 'sheet'?

answers.text: Players once swept and slid stones across a flat sheet of natural pond ice
The first rinks were marked out with bedsheets
It is short for 'sheet of granite' from the stones' source

questions.fun_fact: Curling began on frozen Scottish lochs, and 'sheet' simply described the smooth expanse of ice a match was played on. The term survived indoors even though modern sheets are carefully prepared and 'pebbled' with sprayed water droplets.

questions.question: The badminton and tennis term 'let' (a replayed point) shares an origin with which old meaning of the word?

answers.text: 'To hinder' or obstruct, as in 'without let or hindrance'
'To allow', as in letting someone serve again
'To rent', from leasing a court

questions.fun_fact: The archaic 'let' meaning obstruction survives almost only in racket sports and legal phrasing. A serve that clips the net is 'hindered' on its way, so the point is replayed; the everyday meaning of 'let' as 'allow' is a completely separate, opposite word.

questions.question: Why was the basketball 'dribble' originally a bounce pass to oneself, invented to get around which rule?

answers.text: The early rule banned running while holding the ball
Players were not allowed to pass to a teammate twice in a row
The ball could not be thrown above shoulder height

questions.fun_fact: Naismith's first rules forbade running with the ball, so trapped players bounced it ahead and chased it as a legal way to advance. Coaches initially saw dribbling as a desperate last resort rather than the core skill it became.

questions.question: The word 'stadium' originally referred to what, before it meant a sporting arena?

answers.text: A unit of distance, the length of a Greek footrace
The wooden benches spectators sat on
The starting block carved from stone

questions.fun_fact: A 'stadion' was about 180 metres, the length of the original sprint at Olympia. The track took the name of the distance, and eventually the whole arena built around it inherited the word 'stadium'.

questions.question: Why is a knockdown in boxing counted to ten specifically, rather than any other number?

answers.text: The Queensberry rules picked ten seconds as a fair recovery window
It matched the ten rounds of early championship bouts
Ten was the number of judges originally seated ringside

questions.fun_fact: Before the count, a downed bare-knuckle fighter simply had 30 seconds and a chalk 'scratch' line to toe. The ten-second count, codified in the 1860s, created the dramatic, suspenseful tradition of the referee's count we know today.

questions.question: The hockey term 'puck' is believed to derive from a word in which sport's vocabulary?

answers.text: Hurling, where 'to puck' means to strike the ball
Cricket, from 'puck' meaning a hard knock
Lacrosse, from an Indigenous word for disc

questions.fun_fact: In the Irish game of hurling, 'to puck' the sliotar means to hit it sharply. Irish immigrants helped shape early ice hockey in Canada, and the flat rubber disc likely inherited the striking word as its name.

questions.question: Why does a golf score of one stroke under par on a hole get called a 'birdie'?

answers.text: From American slang 'bird', meaning something excellent
A bird once flew into a famous winning putt
It was named after golfer Henry Bird

questions.fun_fact: In 1903 a player at Atlantic City said a fine shot was 'a bird of a shot', 1900s American slang for excellent. The 'birdie' caught on, and 'eagle' and 'albatross' were later coined as bigger birds for even better scores.

questions.question: The cricketing term 'over' for a set of six deliveries originally referred to what?

answers.text: The umpire calling 'over' to switch bowling ends
The ball being bowled over the batsman's shoulder
A bowler's run-up crossing over the crease

questions.fun_fact: When a bowler finished a set of balls, the umpire called 'over!' to signal play would switch to the opposite end. The word for the announcement became the word for the unit, even though early overs were four balls, not six.

questions.question: Why is the front-crawl swimming stroke sometimes still called the 'Australian crawl'?

answers.text: Australian swimmers popularised the flutter-kick version around 1900
It was first swum across Sydney Harbour as a stunt
Australia made it compulsory in school swimming

questions.fun_fact: Swimmers like Richmond Cavill in Sydney refined an alternating overarm stroke with a flutter kick that proved far faster than the breaststroke and sidestroke then dominant. The world simply called the speedy new style the 'Australian crawl'.

questions.question: The word 'gymkhana', used for equestrian and motoring skill events, was assembled from languages in which region?

answers.text: British India, blending Hindi-Urdu and English
Colonial East Africa, from Swahili and Portuguese
Persia, from two Farsi words for horse and field

questions.fun_fact: 'Gend-khana' meant a ball-game house in Hindi-Urdu, and British colonials reshaped it into 'gymkhana', mixing in 'gymnasium'. It first described a sports clubhouse before coming to mean the skill-and-obstacle contests held there.

questions.question: Why do football clubs in England traditionally play a 'Boxing Day' fixture on 26 December?

answers.text: It dates to when the holiday gave working-class fans a rare free day to attend
Clubs once gave away boxed gifts to fans that day
It commemorates a famous match played in a boxing ring

questions.fun_fact: Boxing Day was a holiday when servants and workers were given the day off and a 'Christmas box' of money or goods. With the masses suddenly free, football scheduled matches to fill the stands, and the packed festive fixture list became a beloved tradition.

questions.question: A regulation NBA basketball game lasts 48 minutes of clock time. Roughly how long is the ball actually in live play?

answers.text: About 48 minutes — but the average game takes well over two hours of real time
About 90 minutes once stoppages and replays are counted
About 20 minutes, the rest being free throws and timeouts

questions.fun_fact: The 48 minutes of game clock stretch into roughly 2 hours 15 minutes of wall-clock time because the clock stops on every whistle, free throw, timeout and substitution — so under half the broadcast is live action.

questions.question: In American football, studies of broadcasts have measured how much actual ball-in-play action a typical three-hour NFL game contains. Roughly how much is it?

answers.text: About 11 minutes
About 35 minutes
About 60 minutes

questions.fun_fact: A Wall Street Journal study clocked the average play at around 4 seconds, with about 130 plays per game — totalling roughly 11 minutes of action inside a broadcast that runs three hours, most of which is replays and players standing around.

questions.question: Which event does this photograph from the 1936 Olympics show?

answers.text: Long jump
Pole vault
Hurdles

questions.fun_fact: Jesse Owens won four gold medals in Berlin. In the long jump it was his German rival Luz Long who advised him before the final attempt — the two left the stadium arm in arm.

questions.question: Which boxer refused the draft in 1967 and lost three and a half years of his career for it?

answers.text: Joe Frazier
Muhammad Ali
George Foreman

questions.fun_fact: Ali took Olympic gold in Rome in 1960 and the heavyweight title three times. The US Supreme Court overturned his conviction in 1971.

questions.question: Which sport is being played in this 1916 photograph?

answers.text: Cricket
Golf
Baseball

questions.fun_fact: Babe Ruth started out as a pitcher and only then became the most famous hitter in the game. His move from Boston to New York is still called the most consequential transfer in baseball history.

questions.question: Which race did this man win in 1920?

answers.text: The Tour de France
The Berlin Marathon
The Le Mans 24 Hours

questions.fun_fact: Philippe Thys won the Tour three times. Riders had no support crews then: a mechanical was yours to fix, and a broken frame meant a walk to the nearest forge.

questions.question: Which sport did this French player make popular in the 1920s?

answers.text: Hockey
Badminton
Tennis

questions.fun_fact: Suzanne Lenglen lost exactly one match between 1919 and 1926. She played in a calf-length skirt without a corset and with bare forearms — to a 1920 crowd nearly as startling as her strokes.

questions.question: How many metres long is a marathon?
questions.fun_fact: 42,195 metres. The odd 195 come from the 1908 London Games, where the start was moved to Windsor Castle so the royal children could watch.

questions.question: How high above the floor is a basketball hoop?
questions.fun_fact: 3.05 metres — exactly ten feet. James Naismith nailed a peach basket to the gymnasium balcony in 1891, and that is how high the balcony was.

questions.question: How heavy is the men's shot in shot put?
questions.fun_fact: 7.26 kg, which is exactly 16 pounds. The women's shot is 4 kg.

questions.question: How many double stitches make up the seam of a baseball?
questions.fun_fact: 108, every one sewn by hand — no machine has ever been built that can stitch a Major League ball.

questions.question: How high is a tennis net at its centre?
questions.fun_fact: 91.4 cm at the centre and 107 cm at the posts. The sag is deliberate, which is why playing over the middle is the safer shot.
